summary: This informational document contains example traces of EDHOC exchanges. Implementers can use them to check that their code produces the expected messages.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher shows a worked example of a math problem step by step. This is the worked example for the EDHOC handshake, so builders can check theirs.

subtitle: Annotated examples of the EDHOC handshake showing every step and intermediate value.

tldr.problem: Developers implementing EDHOC (Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE) need to verify their implementations produce correct protocol messages. Without reference examples, it is hard to debug cryptographic operations and message encoding.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides two complete, annotated traces of EDHOC protocol execution with every input, output, and intermediate cryptographic value shown step-by-step in hexadecimal and CBOR diagnostic notation.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can compare their output at each protocol step against the reference traces to find bugs. The traces have been verified by two independent implementations, ensuring correctness.

facts.value: NIST P-256 for key exchange and static DH

today: RFC 9529 is an Informational RFC containing test vectors for RFC 9528 (EDHOC). It serves as a reference for implementers. EDHOC is used in constrained IoT environments and is part of IETF standardization for lightweight key exchange. The traces in this RFC are essential for interoperability testing.

sections.title: Purpose and Structure
sections.content:
RFC 9529 contains worked examples (called traces) of complete EDHOC protocol exchanges. EDHOC is a lightweight authenticated key exchange designed for highly constrained devices like embedded IoT systems. This document helps implementers verify their implementations by providing reference outputs at every step.

The document specifies each protocol message before and after encoding in CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation), along with all intermediate cryptographic computations. Every value is shown both as a raw hexadecimal byte string and as a CBOR data item in diagnostic notation.

Two independent implementations have verified the traces, ensuring they are correct. The traces cover different authentication methods, cipher suites, and elliptic curves to provide comprehensive coverage.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a worked example. When you are building EDHOC, you run through the same steps the trace shows and compare your answers at each checkpoint. If they match all the way, your code is correct.

sections.title: Two Scenarios: Signatures and Static DH
sections.content:
The first trace demonstrates authentication with digital signatures. Both the Initiator (the client starting the handshake) and the Responder (the server) authenticate using EdDSA signatures over X.509 certificates. They use cipher suite 0, which selects AES-CCM for encryption, SHA-256 for hashing, and X25519 for the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The certificates are identified by their hash values (the 'x5t' header parameter).

The second trace demonstrates authentication with static Diffie-Hellman keys and shows cipher suite negotiation. The Initiator offers multiple cipher suites, and the Responder selects the one it prefers. Both endpoints authenticate using static DH keys instead of signatures, with the keys identified by short key identifiers (kid). They use NIST P-256 for both the ephemeral and static key agreement. This trace also shows very compact message sizes: 39, 45, and 19 bytes, demonstrating EDHOC's efficiency for constrained networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Trace 1 shows two people signing with their keys to prove who they are. Trace 2 shows them negotiating which encryption method to use, then proving their identity by computing a secret together.

sections.title: How to Read the Traces
sections.content:
Each trace is organized by EDHOC message. For message_1 (the Initiator's first message), the trace lists the method, chosen cipher suite, ephemeral public key, and connection identifier. It shows the Initiator's ephemeral private key in the trace, allowing readers to follow the key derivation.

For message_2 (the Responder's response), the trace shows the Responder's ephemeral key pair, the Diffie-Hellman shared secret computation, the key derivation steps (PRK), the cryptographic authentication computation (MAC), the Responder's signature or static key, and the constructed message.

For message_3 (the Initiator's response) and message_4 (the Responder's confirmation), similar details are provided.

Intermediate values are shown multiple ways:

  • Raw Value: Hexadecimal bytes
  • CBOR Data Item: The same value encoded in CBOR. CBOR diagnostic notation shows the structure clearly

The traces include the final keying material (PRK_out and PRK_exporter) derived for use in OSCORE or other applications, showing what an implementation should produce after the handshake completes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is broken down into pieces. You will see: the raw bytes, the CBOR encoding, how they were computed, and what the next step produces. Follow along step by step.

sections.title: Using Traces for Implementation Testing
sections.content:
An implementer should follow this approach: parse the input values (keys, identifiers, cipher suite parameters) from the trace, run their EDHOC implementation with those inputs, and compare the output at each message and intermediate calculation.

The trace includes explicit CBOR encodings, which is important because EDHOC is transport-independent and messages may be prepended with connection identifiers or other framing depending on the transport protocol. The values shown in the traces assume no such framing.

Hexadecimal values in the trace allow byte-for-byte comparison. CBOR diagnostic notation helps developers understand the logical structure of each message, making it easier to spot encoding errors versus cryptographic errors.

The traces explicitly distinguish between the message sent over the wire (with CBOR encoding) and the logical values (in diagnostic notation). This distinction is critical because EDHOC messages are CBOR sequences or CBOR arrays, and incorrect CBOR encoding is a common implementation error.

The document also includes a section on invalid traces, showing examples of messages that fail due to encoding errors, cryptographic validation failures, or non-canonical CBOR encoding, which can help implementers understand what errors their code should detect.
sections.plainLanguage: To check your code: run it with the same inputs as the trace, print your answers at each step, and compare them to the trace. If they all match, your implementation is correct.

sections.title: Credentials and Key Material
sections.content:
The traces include the complete cryptographic material needed to produce the examples. For the signature-based trace, the X.509 certificates are provided, showing the Initiator and Responder identities, their public keys, and the signature from the issuing CA. The EdDSA public keys are embedded in the certificates.

For the static DH trace, the static DH key pairs are provided in raw form (uncompressed, in hexadecimal).

Ephemeral key pairs are generated fresh for each trace. The documents shows both the private and public ephemeral keys so readers can verify the key generation and scalar multiplication operations used in the Diffie-Hellman computation.

All cryptographic operations (key derivation, hashing, MAC computation, signature generation) are shown with their inputs and outputs, allowing an implementer to verify each step of their implementation independently.
sections.plainLanguage: The trace gives you all the secret keys you need to reproduce the example. Keep them secret in real life, but use them here to verify your implementation works.
